title: Venn diagram examples: who wants both pizza toppings?
description: Five friends order pizza, but adding two topping lists counts Maya twice. Read the circles, find the overlap and see how to count each friend once.

sections.title: Two circles can save a pizza order
sections.html:
A Venn diagram shows how groups relate. In a two-circle example, the overlapping middle holds the things that belong to both groups. OpenStax explains the diagram’s role in making those relationships visible.

Imagine ordering pizza for five friends. One circle means “likes mushrooms”; the other means “likes olives”. A friend can belong to either group, both groups or neither. The circles describe preferences, not separate tables to sit at.

sections.title: Maya is not two people
sections.html:
Here is a small Venn diagram example you can sketch:

  • Mushrooms: Maya, Leo and Sam.
  • Olives: Maya and Noor.
  • Neither: Tess.

Put Maya in the shared middle, Leo and Sam in mushrooms only, and Noor in olives only. Tess stays outside both circles, inside a box representing all five friends.

The middle is the intersection: the members both groups share. Maya still gets one place in the drawing. She has two preferences, not a spare head.

sections.title: Why 3 + 2 does not make five topping fans
sections.html:
Three friends like mushrooms and two like olives. Add those totals and you count Maya twice. To find everyone who likes at least one topping, count her once:

3 + 2 − 1 = 4 friends.

This combined group is the union. OpenStax’s counting rule subtracts the overlap after adding the two group totals.

If you already wrote the separate regions instead—two in mushrooms only, one in both and one in olives only—add 2 + 1 + 1. Do not subtract Maya again. The wording matters, just as it does with “and” and “or”.

sections.title: Do not forget the friend outside
sections.html:
Tess has not vanished because she dislikes both toppings. The rectangle sets the whole group being considered; here that is five friends. Four like at least one topping, leaving one who likes neither.

For your next sketch, try “likes tea” and “likes coffee”. Label the circles before placing anyone. Read each region once, and the little picture will keep your guest list honest.

questions.prompt: Where does Maya go if she likes mushrooms and olives?
questions.explanation: The overlapping middle is the intersection: Maya belongs to both preference groups.

questions.prompt: Three friends like mushrooms, two like olives, and one likes both. How many like at least one topping?
questions.explanation: Add the group totals and subtract the one shared person: 3 + 2 − 1 = 4.

questions.prompt: The separate regions contain 2 in mushrooms only, 1 in both and 1 in olives only. How many like at least one?
questions.explanation: These are separate regions, so 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. The overlap has not been counted twice; do not subtract it again.
